repos.title: Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks
repos.paper_summary: Sentence-BERT (SBERT) modifies BERT to generate fixed-size sentence embeddings suitable for cosine similarity, reducing the time to find the most similar pair in a collection of 10,000 sentences from approximately 65 hours to about 5 seconds. The method adds a pooling operation to the BERT output and fine-tunes the network using siamese or triplet structures on Natural Language Inference data. On seven Semantic Textual Similarity tasks, SBERT achieves an average Spearman rank correlation of 74.89, outperforming InferSent by 11.7 points and Universal Sentence Encoder by 5.5 points. For supervised STS benchmark evaluation, SBERT reaches 84.67 Spearman correlation, comparable to the BERT cross-encoder baseline of 84.30. On SentEval transfer learning tasks, SBERT improves the average accuracy by 2.1 points over InferSent. A limitation is that SBERT underperforms the BERT cross-encoder on the Argument Facet Similarity dataset in cross-topic settings, where it drops by about 7 points because it cannot directly compare unseen argumentative contexts.

repos.title: SkillOpt: Executive Strategy for Self-Evolving Agent Skills
repos.paper_summary: SkillOpt is a text-space optimizer that trains one agent skill document, a natural-language procedure added to the context of a frozen target model. A separate frontier optimizer model reads scored rollouts from a training split and proposes add, delete, or replace edits. A candidate skill is kept only if it raises the score on a held-out selection split. Stability controls include a cap on edits per step (the "textual learning rate"), a buffer of rejected edits passed to later reflection calls, and an epoch-wise slow/meta update. The paper reports results on six benchmarks, seven target models, and three execution modes (direct chat, Codex, Claude Code). For GPT–5.5 in direct chat, the average gain over no skill is +23.5 points, and the average margin over the strongest per-cell baseline is +5.4 points. Exported skills are 300–2,000 tokens, built from 11–44 accepted edits. The paper also reports transfer across model scales and harnesses, and to Omni-MATH. Limitations: the method optimizes one skill for one domain, and it depends on a separate frontier optimizer model. The provided text ends before the slow/meta update is described, so that component and its ablation results are not covered here.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: SkillOpt optimizes an agent's skill document as external state, with validation-gated edits and no weight updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior skill work mainly builds or evolves skill libraries, while prompt optimizers target prompts rather than a persistent skill.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Each step edits the skill with bounded add, delete and replace operations, accepted only if held-out selection score strictly improves.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: SkillOpt is best or tied on all 52 evaluated cells, lifting GPT–5.5 by 23.5 points in direct chat.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Compact skills optimized this way transfer across model scales, harnesses and a nearby benchmark without weight updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix lists the optimizer prompt contracts, limitations, and experimental protocol with patch and split details.

repos.title: Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism
repos.paper_summary: The paper presents Megatron-LM, a method for training multi-billion parameter transformer language models using intra-layer model parallelism in PyTorch. The approach partitions the self-attention and MLP blocks across GPUs by splitting weight matrices column-wise for the first linear layer and row-wise for the second, requiring only two all-reduce operations per forward pass. This design avoids custom compilers and is orthogonal to pipeline parallelism. On 512 NVIDIA V100 GPUs, an 8.3 billion parameter GPT-2 model sustains 15.1 PetaFLOPs with 76% scaling efficiency relative to a single-GPU baseline. The same architecture trains a 3.9 billion parameter BERT variant, where rearranging layer normalization before residual connections prevents degradation observed in standard BERT at larger scales. The 8.3B GPT-2 model achieves a WikiText103 perplexity of 10.8 and LAMBADA accuracy of 66.5%, while the 3.9B BERT model reaches 90.9% accuracy on RACE. Limitations include the requirement for high-bandwidth interconnects like NVLink or InfiniBand, and the fact that the BERT results are reported on development sets for most tasks except RACE.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Megatron-LM trains transformers up to 8.3 billion parameters with intra-layer model parallelism, reaching 76% scaling efficiency on 512 GPUs.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Challenges
digest_headlines.headline: Existing model parallel methods need custom compilers or pipeline changes, so the authors modify only a PyTorch transformer.

digest_headlines.heading: Model Parallel Transformers
digest_headlines.headline: The MLP and attention blocks are split across GPUs so each transformer layer needs only four all-reduce operations.

digest_headlines.heading: Setup
digest_headlines.headline: GPT-2 and BERT models train on an aggregated 174 GB deduplicated corpus with fixed optimizer and learning-rate schedules.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Model parallel scaling reaches 77% of linear scaling at 8.3 billion parameters, and GPT-2 and BERT results set new SOTA marks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that intra-layer parallelism scales to 8.3 billion parameters and suggest hybrid parallelism for larger models.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists BERT finetuning hyperparameters, hybrid parallelism and random number details, text samples, evaluation methodology, and strong scaling results.

repos.title: Video-MME: The First-Ever Comprehensive Evaluation Benchmark of Multi-modal LLMs in Video Analysis
repos.paper_summary:
Video-MME is a manually annotated benchmark of 900 videos and 2,700 multiple-choice questions for evaluating multi-modal large language models on video analysis. The dataset covers six visual domains across 30 subfields, with video durations ranging from 11 seconds to 1 hour. Each video is paired with subtitles and audio tracks where available. Annotators created three four-option questions per video covering perception, reasoning, and information synopsis tasks. A quality review filtered out questions answerable from text alone, reducing the question-only accuracy of Gemini 1.5 Pro to less than 15%.

The paper evaluates commercial models (GPT-4V, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro) and open-source models (VILA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT-Video, Chat-UniVi-V1.5). Gemini 1.5 Pro achieves the highest overall accuracy at 75.0%, followed by GPT-4o at 71.9% and VILA-1.5 at 59.0%. Adding subtitles improves Gemini 1.5 Pro's accuracy by 6.2 points on average; adding audio improves it by 4.3 points. Performance declines as video duration increases for all models tested.

repos.title: Grounded SAM: Assembling Open-World Models for Diverse Visual Tasks
repos.paper_summary: Grounded SAM is a pipeline that combines Grounding DINO and the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to perform open-vocabulary detection and segmentation. Given an image and a text prompt, Grounding DINO generates bounding boxes for the described objects, which serve as box prompts for SAM to produce pixel-level masks. The paper demonstrates that this assembly enables diverse tasks by integrating additional models: RAM or BLIP for automatic dense annotation without user text input, Stable Diffusion for controllable image editing via inpainting, and OSX for instance-specific 3D human mesh recovery. On the Segmentation in the Wild (SGinW) zero-shot benchmark, Grounded SAM with Grounding DINO-Base and SAM-Huge achieves a mean AP of 48.7, outperforming unified models like UNINEXT-H (42.1) and OpenSeeD-L (36.7). A limitation is that performance depends on the accuracy of the initial detection step; if Grounding DINO misses an object, SAM cannot segment it. Additionally, the pipeline requires multiple model invocations, increasing computational overhead compared to single-model approaches.

repos.title: Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows
repos.paper_summary:
Swin Transformer is a hierarchical vision Transformer backbone that computes self-attention within non-overlapping local windows, shifting the window partition by $(\lfloor M/2 \rfloor, \lfloor M/2 \rfloor)$ between consecutive layers to enable cross-window connections while maintaining linear computational complexity with respect to image size. The architecture splits images into $4 \times 4$ patches and progressively merges them across four stages to produce feature maps at resolutions of $H/4$, $H/8$, $H/16$, and $H/32$. A relative position bias is added to the attention scores, parameterized by a matrix of size $(2M-1) \times (2M-1)$.

On ImageNet-1K, Swin-L achieves 87.3% top-1 accuracy after pre-training on ImageNet-22K. For object detection on COCO test-dev, it reaches 58.7 box AP and 51.1 mask AP, surpassing previous best results by +2.7 box AP and +2.6 mask AP. On ADE20K semantic segmentation, it obtains 53.5 mIoU, an improvement of +3.2 mIoU over the prior best model. Ablations show that shifted windows contribute +1.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K and +2.8 mIoU on ADE20K compared to static windows. The cyclic-shift implementation for efficient batch computation provides a 13–18% speed-up over naive padding.

repos.title: FinRL: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Library for Automated Stock Trading in Quantitative Finance
repos.paper_summary:
FinRL is an open-source Python library for automated stock trading using deep reinforcement learning. It structures the workflow into three layers: a market environment simulator, a set of pre-configured DRL agents, and application modules for single-stock, multi-stock, and portfolio allocation tasks. The environment layer models trading as a Markov Decision Process using historical data from six indices (NASDAQ-100, DJIA, S&P 500, HSI, SSE 50, CSI 300) at daily, hourly, or minute granularity. Agents include DQN, DDPG, PPO, SAC, A2C, and TD3, built on OpenAI Baselines and Stable Baselines.

The library incorporates market frictions such as transaction costs, bid-ask spreads, and a turbulence index to control risk during extreme volatility. Backtesting uses the `pyfolio` package. In demonstrations over 2019–2020 data, PPO-based single-stock strategies achieved Sharpe ratios between 1.10 and 1.49, outperforming the S&P 500 baseline of 0.74. For DJIA constituents, TD3 and DDPG strategies yielded Sharpe ratios of 1.38 and 1.28, respectively, exceeding the min-variance baseline of 0.44. Limitations include reliance on historical data that may not reflect future market regimes and the computational cost of training multiple agent configurations.

repos.title: KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
repos.paper_summary: Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KANs) replace the linear weights of multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) with learnable univariate functions to improve accuracy and interpretability. Each edge in a KAN is parameterized as a B-spline combined with a fixed basis function, while nodes simply sum incoming signals. The authors prove that for smooth functions admitting such a representation, approximation error scales favorably with network depth and width compared to standard MLPs. On toy function fitting tasks, smaller KANs achieve comparable or better accuracy than larger MLPs, particularly on high-dimensional data with compositional structures. For example, on a 20-dimensional function, a KAN with 1,000 parameters outperforms an MLP with 10,000 parameters. In PDE solving, KANs approximate solutions to the Poisson equation with lower error than MLPs at similar model sizes. The paper also demonstrates interpretability by using KANs to rediscover mathematical and physical laws in knot theory and Anderson localization. A major limitation is training speed; KANs are approximately 10 times slower than MLPs with the same number of parameters because distinct activation functions prevent batch computation optimizations. Additionally, the theoretical guarantees apply specifically to smooth functions, whereas the original Kolmogorov–Arnold theorem permits non-smooth representations that may be harder to learn.

repos.title: OmniVoice: Towards Omnilingual Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech with Diffusion Language Models
repos.paper_summary:
OmniVoice is a zero-shot text-to-speech model covering over 600 languages. It is a single-stage non-autoregressive model: a bidirectional Transformer trained with a discrete masked diffusion objective maps text directly to 8-codebook acoustic tokens. Full-codebook random masking samples a mask for every token entry, so about 50% of tokens contribute to the loss, compared with one codebook per example in per-layer masking. The backbone is initialized from Qwen3-0.6B weights. The multilingual model trains on 581k hours from 50 open-source datasets.

On LibriSpeech-PC test-clean, it scores 0.729 SIM-o, 1.30 WER and 4.28 UTMOS, against 0.694, 1.59 and 4.28 for CosyVoice3. A bilingual variant trained on Emilia beats F5-TTS, ZipVoice and MaskGCT trained on the same corpus. Subjective SMOS is 3.80 versus 3.65 for Qwen3-TTS. On the 24-language MiniMax benchmark, Chinese character error rate is 1.008 versus 2.252 for MiniMax. Limitations: most baselines use different, larger training data; Cantonese word error rate is 17.709; and the FLEURS-102 results are not in the provided text.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing zero-shot speech models cover few languages, and two-stage discrete pipelines suffer error propagation and information bottlenecks.

digest_headlines.heading: Proposed Method
digest_headlines.headline: Full-codebook random masking and LLM initialization form the method, trained on more than 600 languages from 581k hours of audio.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Models are compared on Chinese, English and multilingual benchmarks using speaker similarity, error rates and subjective listening scores.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Results
digest_headlines.headline: OmniVoice gets the lowest word error rate on LibriSpeech-PC test-clean, at 1.30, and the highest subjective similarity score, at 3.80, among compared models.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that the single-stage design, masking and LLM initialization together give broad language coverage and efficient inference.
